title: Service Discovery
description: Understand client-side vs server-side service discovery, DNS-based approaches, and the stale registry problem that causes cascading failures in production.

segments.text: In a monolith, you know where everything is. In microservices with auto-scaling, services come and go constantly. An order service needs to call inventory, but inventory just scaled from three instances to twelve. How does order service know which twelve IP addresses to call?

Client-side discovery: the calling service queries a registry, gets all available instances, and picks one. Netflix Eureka pioneered this. Each service registers itself on startup, sends heartbeats every thirty seconds, and the caller uses a client library like Ribbon to load-balance across instances.

Server-side discovery: a load balancer sits between services. The caller just calls a single DNS name. AWS ALB does this — it health-checks targets and routes traffic. The caller doesn't need to know about individual instances at all. Simpler client code, but the load balancer becomes a bottleneck.

DNS-based discovery with HashiCorp Consul gives you the best of both worlds. Services register with Consul, and discovery happens via DNS queries. payment.service.consul resolves to healthy instances. But DNS TTL caching can bite you — stale records pointing to dead instances.

Health checking is where this gets subtle. A service can be reachable but not healthy — maybe its database connection pool is exhausted. You need deep health checks: can this service actually serve requests? Shallow checks just verify the process is alive. Kubernetes distinguishes between liveness and readiness probes for exactly this reason.

The stale registry problem is a production killer. Service crashes, heartbeat stops, but the registry takes ninety seconds to evict it. During those ninety seconds, callers are still routing traffic to a dead instance. Netflix saw this cause cascading failures during AWS outages.

Here's a Staff-level question. The registry has stale entries during an outage. You can make eviction faster, but that risks false positives during network partitions — healthy services getting removed. How would you solve this?
segments.thought_prompt: How do you balance fast eviction against false-positive deregistration during network partitions?

segments.text: Kubernetes solved this differently. A Service object is a stable virtual IP. Behind it, Endpoints track which pods are ready. When a pod fails its readiness probe, kube-proxy removes it from the endpoint list within seconds. No separate registry needed — discovery is built into the platform.

Trade-off summary. Eureka: AP system, eventually consistent, survives partitions but stale reads. Consul: CP system, strongly consistent, but unavailable during leader election. Kubernetes Services: tight platform integration, but you're locked into Kubernetes. Choose based on your consistency requirements.

Think about multi-region. If your services span three AWS regions, service discovery needs to work across regions too. But do you want cross-region discovery, or regional isolation with explicit routing?
segments.thought_prompt: Should service discovery be global or regional? What are the failure implications of each?

segments.text: Service discovery is the nervous system of microservices. Get it wrong and services can't find each other. Get it too slow and stale entries cause cascading failures. In production, combine health checking with circuit breakers — even if discovery gives you a bad address, the circuit breaker trips fast and routes elsewhere.
